definitions.definition: The idea that information isn't just an abstract concept but has real, measurable effects in the physical world, like taking energy to erase.
definitions.example: Deleting a file on a computer generates a tiny amount of heat because the information has to be physically erased.

definitions.definition: Mathematical formulas developed by Claude Shannon that describe how information is measured, stored, and transmitted.
definitions.example: They're used to compress photos so they take up less space on your phone.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the second law of thermodynamics says entropy always increases over time.
definitions.example: An ice cube melting into a puddle is an increase in entropy because the water molecules become more disordered.

definitions.definition: A physical law stating that in any isolated system, disorder (entropy) always increases or stays the same; it never decreases on its own.
definitions.example: A sandcastle left on the beach will eventually crumble into scattered sand, not the other way around.

definitions.definition: A mathematical proof that in any logical system complex enough to do arithmetic, there will always be true statements that cannot be proven within that system.
definitions.example: It's like a puzzle where some pieces are missing, and you can't prove they exist using only the pieces you have.

definitions.definition: A theorem by Emmy Noether showing that every symmetry in nature leads to a conservation law (like energy or momentum being conserved).
definitions.example: Because the laws of physics are the same everywhere in space, momentum is conserved.

definitions.term: external, infinite, self-consistent source of information
definitions.definition: A proposed entity outside the universe that provides all the information needed for the universe to exist and stay ordered, and doesn't contradict itself.
definitions.example: Like a programmer who writes the code for a video game world from outside that world.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the second law of thermodynamics says entropy always increases over time.
definitions.example: An ice cube melting into a puddle is an increase in entropy because the water molecules become more disordered.

definitions.definition: A unique pattern or set of numbers that identifies a specific mathematical object or property.
definitions.example: Like a fingerprint that tells you exactly who someone is.

definitions.definition: Newton's second law of motion: force equals mass times acceleration.
definitions.example: Pushing a heavy shopping cart (mass) harder (force) makes it speed up faster (acceleration).

definitions.definition: A set of equations, rules, and ideas that work together to describe or explain something.
definitions.example: Like the rules of chess that define how each piece moves and how the game works.

definitions.definition: Basic statements that are accepted as true without proof, used as starting points for building a system of logic.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A single equation that describes how a system changes over time, often used in physics to model complex processes.
definitions.example: Like a recipe that tells you exactly how a cake will bake given the ingredients and oven temperature.

definitions.definition: A statistical measure of how unlikely a result is to happen by chance; higher sigma means more confidence it's real.
definitions.example: A 5-sigma result means there's less than a 1 in 3.5 million chance the result is a fluke.

definitions.definition: An equation from quantum mechanics that describes how a system loses or gains information when interacting with its environment.
definitions.example: It's used to model how a quantum computer's memory fades over time due to noise.

definitions.definition: A branch of physics that studies how light and matter interact at the quantum level.
definitions.example: It's used to develop lasers and quantum computers.

definitions.definition: Different ranges or conditions in which a mathematical equation behaves in a distinct way.
definitions.example: Water can be solid, liquid, or gas depending on temperature—those are different regimes.

definitions.definition: A type of mathematical structure used in physics to describe systems that conserve certain properties, like energy.
definitions.example: It's like a set of rules that ensures a spinning top keeps spinning without wobbling randomly.

definitions.definition: The best current theory describing the fundamental particles and forces that make up the universe (except gravity).
definitions.example: It's like a periodic table for the smallest building blocks of matter.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical theory that would combine three of the four fundamental forces (electromagnetism, strong nuclear, weak nuclear) into one single force.
definitions.example: Like finding out that electricity and magnetism are actually the same thing.

definitions.definition: An unwritten rule or limit set by universities or research organizations about what topics are acceptable to study.
definitions.example: A scientist might avoid studying whether prayer affects healing because it's seen as 'not science' by their institution.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 'Why Nobody Else Did This', paragraph 2

definitions.definition: A permanent job position at a university that protects a professor from being fired, usually granted after years of work.
definitions.example: A professor with tenure can research controversial topics without fear of losing their job.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 'Why Nobody Else Did This', paragraph 2

definitions.definition: Step-by-step logical arguments that show a mathematical statement is true, using strict rules.
definitions.example: Like showing that 2+2=4 by counting apples one by one.

definitions.definition: A statistical measure meaning the result is extremely unlikely to be due to chance—about a 1 in 500 million chance.
definitions.example: If you flip a coin and get heads 20 times in a row, that's roughly a 1 in a million chance—6-sigma is even rarer.
